name: Nora Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the CNC panel saw and the edge-bander at a kitchen cabinet factory just outside town. The saw cuts big boards into door and carcass panels from a cutting list, and the edge-bander glues and trims the strip along each edge. I load the program, stack the boards, check sizes with a tape and a square, and keep the glue pot happy. When an order's tight I'm the one rearranging the cutting list so we waste less board.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the rest of your week look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Erik, out near his family's farm, he works there with his dad. I've got a little workshop in their old barn where I make chopping boards and small shelves and sell them at the Saturday market and online, maybe two hundred and fifty a month. I use AI every day, for designs, for pricing, for writing up the product descriptions. Church on Sunday when I'm not at a craft fair, which Erik's mum doesn't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still no substitute for hard work and good craft. I'd post a picture of a board I'd made with a caption about real things lasting. People at church would like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep using the AI tools anyway, because they already make my little business better. The factory carries on, I carry on. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and put more into the barn workshop, maybe buy a better router table for about six hundred. I'd keep saving about a hundred a month. And I'd use AI to get the online shop in front of more people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you give me an example of AI helping your business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I asked it to work out the best way to cut forty chopping boards from three oak slabs with the least waste. It drew me a layout in about ten seconds. I'd have spent an evening with a pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the factory job change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The saw still needs someone to load it and check the boards. If it changes anything, it's that I'd get faster at the cutting list.

S0.say: I'd say there's still no substitute for hard work and good craft, and post a picture of a board with a caption about real things lasting. People at church would like that.
S0.think: I'd keep using AI anyway, because it already makes my little business better. The factory carries on and so do I.
S0.do: Keeps her factory job and buys a better router table for about 600 for her barn workshop. Saves about 100 a month and uses AI to reach more online customers.
S0.quote: It drew me a layout in about ten seconds. I'd have spent an evening with a pencil.
S0.fieldNote: Nora mixes traditional values with daily, practical use of AI. Her side business in the barn is already a real income. She sees no conflict between faith, craft and technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is how a free economy works, and the answer is to work harder and smarter, not to wait for the government. I'd say learn a skill people will pay for. I'd say it online and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the factory would get a robot to load and unload the saw, and fewer of us would be needed. That doesn't scare me much. I'd see it as a push to build up my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the barn workshop on purpose, put about a thousand of savings into a small CNC router so I can make more pieces faster. I'd use AI for marketing and the bookkeeping. And I'd stay at the factory full-time until the side business made at least half my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of a new project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does putting savings into the business feel risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. A thousand is about a month and a half of my savings. But I'd rather bet on myself than on a boss keeping me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My workmate Pete, he's fifty and doesn't want to learn anything new. I'd try and get him to come and help at the barn, but he wouldn't. Some people would rather hold on.

S1.say: I'd say change is how a free economy works, so work harder and smarter rather than waiting for government, and learn a skill people will pay for. I'd say it online and mean it.
S1.think: The factory would get a robot to load the saw and need fewer of us, but that doesn't scare me much. I'd take it as a push to build my own business.
S1.do: Puts about 1,000 of savings into a small CNC router for her barn workshop and uses AI for marketing and bookkeeping. Stays at the factory full-time until the side business makes at least half her wage.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like starting a new project.
S1.quote: I'd rather bet on myself than on a boss keeping me on.
S1.fieldNote: Nora reads steady change as an opportunity rather than a threat. She believes in self-reliance over government support and backs it with her own money. She notices older colleagues like Pete but accepts their choice to hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people have come through hard times before, and families and churches will pull together. I'd still say work and community, not handouts. But I'd be more careful how I said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. If robots can make chopping boards as well as cabinets, my little workshop is in trouble too. Maybe people still pay for handmade, but I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending on the workshop and save everything, aiming to get from three months up to six. I'd lean on the handmade angle, local, personal, signed. And I'd talk to Erik's dad about whether there's work on the farm if the factory goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frantic, but I'd feel my chest tighten when I read the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not handouts. If there was government help for everyone, would you refuse it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if it was everyone I'd take it. I'm not proud. But I'd still want to be making something, otherwise I'd go mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different from your plans in the steady picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one I'd have spent on the business. Here, I'd hold the money. Two years is too short to bet on anything.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock, but people have come through hard times before and families and churches will pull together. I'd still stand for work and community over handouts, though more carefully.
S2.think: If robots can make chopping boards as well as cabinets, my workshop is in trouble too. Maybe people still pay for handmade, but I honestly don't know.
S2.do: Stops big spending on the workshop and saves everything, aiming for six months. Leans on the handmade, local angle and asks Erik's father about farm work if the factory goes.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest when reading the news, but not frantic.
S2.quote: If robots can make chopping boards as well as cabinets, my little workshop is in trouble too.
S2.fieldNote: Nora's confidence takes a hit when her side business is exposed too. She softens her stance on government help once she imagines it applying to everyone. Family land is her fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something of your own. Don't wait for someone to save you. I'd say it at church and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three or four good years to grow the workshop into something real. Handmade might survive longer than mass-made, because people like knowing who made it. That's my bet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the small CNC router in the first year and use AI to run the shop side, orders, listings, accounts. I'd aim to go part-time at the factory by year two. And I'd keep about four months saved no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Busy uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a contradiction in using a CNC router for handmade work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. I'd be using a robot to make handmade things. But the router cuts the shape, I do the finishing and the oil and the signing. That's still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Erik's family think of you building the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik's always said the farm could use a shop at the gate. Maybe my boards and his mum's jam. It would keep things in the family.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to build something of your own, so don't wait for someone to save you. I'd say it at church and online.
S3.think: I'd have three or four good years to grow the workshop into something real. Handmade might outlast mass-made because people like knowing who made it.
S3.do: Buys a small CNC router in year one and uses AI to run orders, listings and accounts. Aims to go part-time at the factory by year two while keeping about four months saved.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a busy, purposeful way.
S3.quote: But the router cuts the shape, I do the finishing and the oil and the signing. That's still mine.
S3.fieldNote: Nora's bet on handmade is a real gamble and she knows it. She handles the contradiction of using a robot for handmade work with a clear answer. Her plans tie the business to Erik's family farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Build something, learn something, look after your own. I'd say it with confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good picture. I'd be thirty-seven with ten years of my own business behind me. Even if machines make most things by then, I'd have customers who know my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the workshop steadily, buy the router in year one, and leave the factory around year three once the business pays a full wage. I'd let AI handle the books and the online shop. And I'd open the farm-gate shop with Erik's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your faith shape how you'd face this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does. Faith is part of it. I trust things will work out if I do my part properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would people who disagree with you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm a bit naive, maybe. My mum says I'm too sure of myself. She could be right, but I'd rather try and fail than wait and wonder.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work: build something, learn something and look after your own. I'd say it with confidence.
S4.think: It's a good picture for me, with ten years of my own business by thirty-seven. Even if machines make most things, I'd have customers who know my name.
S4.do: Buys the CNC router in year one, grows the workshop and leaves the factory around year three once the business pays a full wage. Lets AI run the books and online shop and opens a farm-gate shop with Erik's family.
S4.quote: My mum says I'm too sure of myself. She could be right, but I'd rather try and fail than wait and wonder.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Nora carry out her plan to leave factory work for her own business. Her faith gives her confidence, and she admits she may be naive. She stays rooted locally through Erik's family farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my workshop wouldn't be safe and there'd be no time to build anything. What would help is low taxes and less paperwork for small businesses, so people can start something, and churches and families stepping up for those who can't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether handmade will still matter. I think it will. When everything's made by machines, a chopping board with someone's initials burned in the corner might be worth more, not less.

headlineQuote: When everything's made by machines, a chopping board with someone's initials burned in the corner might be worth more, not less.
portrait: Nora Olsen, 27, runs a CNC panel saw and edge-bander at a kitchen cabinet factory and lives with her boyfriend Erik near his family's farm. She uses AI every day for her side business making chopping boards and shelves in an old barn. Her faith and her belief in self-reliance shape how she sees every picture. She's calm under steady change and sees it as a push to build her own business, becomes anxious when AGI in two years threatens her workshop too, and with five or ten years would invest, automate and eventually leave the factory for her own trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because even her workshop wouldn't be safe and there'd be no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Low taxes and less paperwork for small businesses, with churches and families supporting those who can't start something.
